deacon noun

late Latin

Tert. Praescr. 3 (Lewis & Short)
Vulg. Phil. 1.1
M-O s.v. deacon

diāconus, diāconī m.

noun, second declension

Greek διάκονος, a servant. The Vulgate also has a third-declension plural, diāconibus (Phil. 1.1); Egeria writes diācones. In both churches the deacon reads the Gospel, leads the prayers of the people and censes.

Other words

  • lēvīta, lēvītae m. — a Levite; a deacon

    noun, first declension · also used · late Latin · Sid. Ep. 9.2 (Lewis & Short); Prud. Perist. 2.39 (Lewis & Short)

    Properly a Levite of the Old Testament; Prudentius gives the name to the deacons Lawrence and Vincent.

Examples

  • Paulus et Tīmotheus, servī Jēsū Chrīstī, omnibus sānctīs in Chrīstō Jēsū, quī sunt Philippīs, cum episcopīs et diāconibus.

    Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons.Vulg. Phil. 1.1

  • et ūnus ex diāconibus facit commemorātiōnem singulōrum, sīcut solet esse cōnsuētūdō

    and one of the deacons makes the commemoration of each person, as the custom isItin. Eger. 24.5

See also priest, bishop, censer, Gospel.
